To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the lack of hospitals with substantial experience in treating strokes and heart attacks is associated with increased mortality, and the addition of such hospitals would reduce mortality.

Japan has fewer hospitals with substantial experience in complex modern medical procedures than the United States, that this is the result of the Japanese health care system, and that it has led to higher mortality rates from strokes and heart attacks.

(1) Japan has a large number of small, primitive hospitals and clinics that are not equipped for modern medical treatment; (2) this proliferation of small hospitals and clinics is the result of the regulatorily-capped prices for the most modern procedures and the subsidized demand for medical treatment; and (3) this proliferation has resulted in a large number of cities that lack hospitals with any substantial expertise in modern medical treatments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the structure of a country's medical system affects the quality of care and, hence, the mortality rate of its population.
the effects of health care reform on health outcomes.
the effects of health insurance on the supply and quality of medical services and on the health outcomes of the insured.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Japan's universal health insurance system has not been cost-effective in the treatment of strokes and heart attacks.
the Japanese health care system has failed to deliver the most advanced and most cost-effective medical treatments to a significant fraction of the Japanese population.
the Japanese system, by capping the prices paid for complex modern medical treatments, appears to have caused a substantial increase in mortality from strokes and heart attacks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Japan’s universal health insurance, by cutting the number of hospitals that specialize in modern medical procedures, has raised the death rate for strokes and heart attacks.

the Japanese system of universal health insurance and regulatorily capped prices has produced a proliferation of small clinics and hospitals that lack the capacity to provide the most modern and complex treatments for heart disease and strokes.
, in Japan, the lack of experience in modern treatment of cerebrovascular and coronary disease is responsible for 10,000 to 20,000 deaths per year, or about 5 percent of all deaths.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the regulatorily-driven lack in Japan of hospitals with substantial experience in treating heart attacks and strokes is costing the lives of hundreds of thousands of Japanese every year.

the Japanese government’s policy of capping the prices it pays for medical procedures, combined with its policy of subsidizing health care demand, has led to the proliferation of small hospitals with little or no expertise in modern procedures.
, while universal health insurance may be a necessary condition for the provision of health care to the poor, it is far from sufficient.
